_note: All samples are synthetic: reserved domains (.example, .test), documentation IPs (192.0.2.0/24, 198.51.100.0/24, 203.0.113.0/24, 2001:db8::/32) and fictional people. expectedLocalVerdict is the result without reputation lookups; expectedSignals are finding kinds (src/engine/config.ts) that must fire. tests/samples.test.ts asserts both.

samples.title: Microsoft 365 password-expiry phish
samples.notes: The second Authentication-Results header (claiming mx.microsoft.com and all-pass) sits below the provider's own and is forged. The bottom Received header is forged too: its timestamp is 12.5 hours after the later hops.

samples.title: Fake recruiter job offer
samples.notes: SPF/DKIM/DMARC all pass, which proves authentication alone is not a verdict. The Gmail local part contains '_' and '-', which Gmail does not allow, so the address cannot belong to a real account.

samples.title: Overdue invoice with HTML and .pdf.exe attachments
samples.notes: Uses the Microsoft 365 / Exchange Online Authentication-Results format, which has no authserv-id. The .pdf.exe starts with the 'MZ' bytes of a Windows program but is plain text, not executable.

samples.title: Ordinary newsletter (control)
samples.notes: Control sample. SPF/DKIM/DMARC pass and align, links match their display text, the private IP is on an internal first hop (normal), and the greeting is personal. Any finding here is a false positive.

samples.title: Unpaid toll text (smishing)
samples.notes: The link has no scheme (bare domain), as is typical in SMS.

samples.title: Google Safe Browsing test URLs (real reputation hit)
samples.notes: Google's official test URLs, not actually malicious. Locally only the google.test brand name is suspicious; with Safe Browsing configured, the match forces High. Still to confirm in M4: which of these two URLs the Lookup API actually matches today.
